# `secrets/high-entropy`: Hardcoded secret, token or password

<!-- Generated by `npm run docs:rules` from the rule metadata in src/rules/. Edit only the
     hand:* regions here; everything else comes from the rule and is overwritten. -->

| Family  | Default severity | GitHub security-severity | CWE                                                                                                                    |
| ------- | ---------------- | ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| secrets | high             | 8.0                      | [CWE-798](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/798.html), [CWE-259](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/259.html) |

Individual findings can have a lower or higher severity than the default, and each has a
confidence (high, medium or low). Both are explained below.

## What it detects

<!-- hand:detects -->

Generic credentials that do not match a known provider format:

- High-entropy string literals bound to a secret-like name (`apiKey`, `jwtSecret`,
  `clientSecret`, `token`, `password`, …) in code, JSON, YAML and committed env files.
- Hardcoded passwords bound to password-like names.
- Hardcoded fallbacks such as `process.env.JWT_SECRET || '…'`.
- Literal keys passed as the key argument of signing and encryption calls (`jwt.sign`,
  `createHmac`, `createCipheriv`, and similar): reported as a hardcoded signing key.

Confidence is **medium** when the name says it is a secret, lower otherwise.

<!-- /hand:detects -->

## Why it matters

A value bound to a secret-like name (apiKey, jwtSecret, password, …) looks like a real credential: it is long, random and not a placeholder. It does not match a known provider format, so VibeGuard cannot be certain; review it. Typical cases are JWT signing secrets, session secrets, webhook secrets and admin passwords.

## Messages

What a finding from this rule says (parameters in braces):

- "{name}" is assigned a high-entropy literal that looks like a real credential.
- "{name}" is assigned a hardcoded password.
- {name}() is called with a hardcoded signing/encryption key.

## How to fix

If it is real: rotate it, read it from a server-side environment variable, and fail fast when it is missing (no hardcoded fallback). Generate signing secrets with a CSPRNG (openssl rand -base64 48). If it is not a secret, rename the variable or add a suppression with the reason.

### Vulnerable

```ts
const JWT_SECRET = process.env.JWT_SECRET || 'k3P9…hardcoded…';
const token = jwt.sign({ sub: user.id }, JWT_SECRET);
```

### Fixed

```ts
const JWT_SECRET = process.env.JWT_SECRET;
if (!JWT_SECRET || JWT_SECRET.length < 32) {
  throw new Error('JWT_SECRET must be set (>= 32 random bytes)');
}
const token = jwt.sign({ sub: user.id }, JWT_SECRET, { expiresIn: '1h' });
```

## False positives and limitations

<!-- hand:false-positives -->

This rule has the highest false-positive risk of the secrets family, which is why its
findings are never high confidence.

- **Names that mean something else** are excluded by whole-word matching: URLs, ids,
  labels, header names, storage key names, length limits, public keys (`publicKey`,
  `passwordMinLength`, `tokenUrl`, `apiKeyHeader`).
- **Placeholders and low-entropy values** (`changeme`, `your-secret`, repeated
  characters) are not reported. URLs, paths and env-variable references are skipped.
- **Test code:** human-chosen strings (`'test-secret'`, `'hunter2!'`) are test data and are
  skipped. Random-looking tokens in tests are reported with lowered confidence.
- **CI and compose files:** throwaway passwords for database service containers are
  skipped when they are human-chosen.
- **Not a secret?** Rename the variable to say what it is, or suppress the finding with
  the reason.
- **Limitations:** a random token in a variable with a neutral name (`const x = '…'`) is
  not reported; values assembled at runtime are missed.

<!-- /hand:false-positives -->

## How to suppress

Only suppress a finding after confirming it is safe. Put the directive on the line above
the reported line (or use `vibeguard-ignore-line` on the line itself, or
`vibeguard-ignore-file` anywhere in the file). The reason is required: a directive without
one suppresses nothing and is reported.

```ts
// vibeguard-ignore-next-line secrets/high-entropy -- explain why this is safe (at least 10 characters)
<the line VibeGuard reported>
```

Use the comment syntax of the file: `//` or `/* */` in code, `#` in `.env` and YAML
files, `--` in SQL.

To turn the rule off or change its severity for the whole project, use `.vibeguard.yml`:

```yaml
version: 1
rules:
  secrets/high-entropy: off # or: { severity: low }
```

See [configuration](../../configuration.md) and
[ADR-0004](../../adr/0004-suppression-design.md).

## CWE

- [CWE-798](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/798.html): Use of Hard-coded Credentials
- [CWE-259](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/259.html): Use of Hard-coded Password
